row.note: The commentary labels naʿbudu with Arabic ʿ-b-d; Deuteronomy uses the cognate Hebrew ʿābad for serving YHWH alone, showing the same service and worship range.
The commentary stresses that the foregrounded “you” excludes every other object of worship; Deut 6:13 commands Israel to fear and serve YHWH alone.
The commentary makes exclusive address the point of “you alone”; the Shema confesses YHWH as Israel’s one God, grounding that exclusivity in Israel’s central creed.
The commentary labels naʿbudu from Arabic ʿ-b-d; Psalm 100 uses Hebrew ʿābad for the community’s joyful service of YHWH as it comes before him with song.
The commentary treats “we” as a community that knows its owner; the psalm names worshippers as God’s people and sheep of his pasture, giving communal service a shepherd-and-flock image.
The commentary’s Arabic ʿ-b-d is cognate with the Hebrew root in “you shall serve God”; Exodus makes service to God the destination of Israel’s release from Egypt.
The commentary recalls Pharaoh’s enslavement of Israel and its reversal in exclusive service to God; Moses is told that the people will serve God on this mountain after leaving Egypt.
The commentary links ʿabd to both belonging and enslavement; Exodus uses the cognate Hebrew service word for Israel’s bitter forced labor under Egypt.
The commentary’s Pharaoh scene treats human mastery as the corrupt form of servitude; Exodus describes the Egyptians making Israel’s life bitter with hard labor.
The commentary calls the worshipper God’s owned servant; Leviticus calls Israelites God’s servants, brought out of Egypt, and forbids selling them as slaves.
The commentary links service with a trodden, guided way; Deut 10:12 puts walking in God’s ways beside serving him with all one’s heart and soul.
The commentary hears a path within service and then asks for guidance; Moses joins walking in God’s ways to loving and serving him wholeheartedly.
The commentary describes worship as an all-encompassing allegiance; Deut 11:13 uses the cognate Hebrew service root in a command to love and serve YHWH with all heart and soul.
The commentary’s naʿbudu and Joshua’s “we will serve YHWH” use cognate Arabic and Hebrew roots for service.
The commentary reads “we” as a worshipping community; Joshua sets rival gods before Israel and declares that he and his household will serve YHWH.
The commentary makes the worshipper’s exclusive choice rule out other masters; Jacob tells his whole household to put away foreign gods before going to Bethel.
The commentary joins service and asking help in one first-person plural prayer; Jacob calls the household to make an altar to the God who answered him in distress and stayed with him on the way.
The commentary contrasts one owner with competing masters; Elijah asks Israel how long it will limp between two opinions and calls for a decision between YHWH and Baal.
The commentary’s fronted “you” excludes all other recipients of worship; the psalmist addresses God as great and says that he alone is God.
The commentary distinguishes asking God for aid from the means used to endure; Psalm 50 joins calling on God in trouble, his deliverance, and the worshipper’s honoring him.
The commentary says God is not a servant or a needy recipient of help; Psalm 50 says God would not need to tell Israel if he were hungry because the world is his.
The commentary leaves the requested aid open to every need; the pilgrim psalm names YHWH, maker of heaven and earth, as the speaker’s help.
The commentary explains service as obedience reaching humility; the psalm calls the community to bow and kneel before its maker.
The commentary’s “we” is a community belonging to one owner; the psalm calls Israel God’s people and the sheep of his hand.
The commentary speaks for a plural worshipping community that asks only God for aid; the psalm tells Israel to trust YHWH, its help and shield.
The commentary moves from praise of God to direct address and exclusive service; Nehemiah’s communal prayer says “you alone” are YHWH, maker of all, while heaven’s host worships you.
The commentary has a praying “we” address God directly for aid; Nehemiah’s communal confession turns to “our God” and asks him to attend to the people’s hardship.
The commentary’s aid includes support for the worn traveler; Isaiah contrasts idols that must be carried with God’s promise to carry and rescue Israel from birth to old age.
The commentary asks why help should be sought from what cannot benefit or save; Isaiah says an idol cannot answer its worshippers or rescue them from trouble.
The commentary says false objects of worship cannot provide aid; in Elijah’s contest Baal’s prophets call and dance, but no voice answers them.
The commentary develops the worked, passable road as an image beside service and guidance; Isaiah calls for a way to be prepared for the Lord’s coming.
The commentary describes a road made easy by being flattened; Isaiah pictures valleys raised and rough ground leveled to make the Lord’s highway passable.
The commentary says the first-person plural community is open to people from different paths; Isaiah includes foreigners who join themselves to YHWH, serve him, and love his name.
The commentary distinguishes God as the one asked for help from human agents who can assist; Aaron and Hur physically support Moses’ hands when he grows tired.
The commentary emphasizes that “you alone” excludes every rival recipient; Jesus answers the tempter by commanding worship and service of the Lord God alone.
The commentary stresses the turn from speaking about God to speaking to him, and the plural “we”; Jesus teaches disciples to begin prayer with “Our Father.”
The commentary says the second “you” separately directs the request for aid to God; the Lord’s Prayer asks the Father for daily bread in the first-person plural.
The commentary joins worship with dependence on God for help; the Lord’s Prayer asks God to deliver the praying community from evil.
The commentary’s ownership section contrasts a person shared by quarrelling owners with one belonging to a single master; Jesus says a slave cannot serve two masters.
The commentary explains worship as belonging and obedience, while also recalling human enslavement; Paul says people become slaves of the one they obey, whether sin or righteousness.
The commentary contrasts belonging to God with being enslaved by human masters; Paul tells believers bought with a price not to become slaves of people.
The commentary’s opening praise calls God Lord of the worlds; Paul proclaims the maker of the world as Lord of heaven and earth.

row.basis: God does not need human service
row.note: The commentary says God has no need of a helper; Paul says God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he gives life and breath to all.
The commentary says service is a state of belonging, not merely a scheduled rite; Paul calls believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice and their life as worship.
The commentary treats aid as an open request addressed to God; Hebrews invites people to approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find help in need.
The commentary reads both verbs as an ongoing state rather than a past act or future promise; Paul’s instruction to pray continually gives that persistence a Christian practice.
The commentary’s “we” speaks directly to God; the gathered believers pray together to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them.
The commentary says aid is separately directed to God; the gathered church asks God to enable his servants to speak boldly amid threats.
The commentary notes that aid among humans can be real while God remains the one finally sought; Paul tells believers to bear one another’s burdens.
The commentary cites Jesus refusing divine status; when Cornelius falls before Peter, Peter raises him and says he too is only a man.
The commentary describes angels rejecting worship directed to them; John falls before an angel, who refuses it and says to worship God.
The commentary’s cited Qur’anic scene has angels deny being objects of worship; Hebrews instead says all God’s angels are to worship the Son, a direct difference over the recipient.

row.basis: worship of God and the Lamb
row.note: The commentary insists on address to God alone and cites Jesus’ rejection of being made divine; Revelation depicts every creature giving blessing and honor to the one on the throne and the Lamb.
The commentary’s exclusive “you” is addressed to God and notes Jesus rejecting divine status; Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as “my Lord and my God,” making the Christological difference explicit.
The commentary says those who belong to God are protected from the adversary; Jesus describes his sheep as his own and says no one will snatch them from his hand.
The commentary understands “we” as a community of God’s servants; Peter calls believers God’s own people, set apart to proclaim his acts.
The commentary notes that Fatiha is recited in every prayer, so even an individual says “we”; the Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times daily.
The commentary distinguishes worship from asking aid while placing both inside prayer; the rabbis interpret “serve him with all your heart” as prayer, treating petition itself as service.
The commentary says worship exceeds scheduled rites but is spoken within ritual prayer; the Talmud relates the fixed prayers to the daily offerings, preserving a sacrificial dimension of prayer.
The commentary’s communal “we” includes earlier generations; the Mishnah teaches each generation to see itself as having come out of Egypt, making inherited history a present first-person identity.
The commentary evokes a traveler whose mount fails and who needs support; Qoheleth says a companion can lift someone who falls, making human aid concrete beneath reliance on God.
The commentary warns that backing someone can aid wrongdoing; Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat for helping the wicked and loving those who hate YHWH.
The commentary presents a community whose “we” can include people of distinct backgrounds; Isaiah says the foreigners who join YHWH will be brought to his house of prayer.
The commentary connects belonging to God’s servants with protection from Satan; Jesus gives his disciples authority over the enemy’s power and danger.
The commentary links service with the straight path and contrasts it with roads that scatter people; Jesus describes the narrow way that leads to life.
The commentary explains service as reaching bodily humility; Paul pictures every knee bending at Jesus’ name, adding a Christian account of universal homage.
The commentary emphasizes the worshipper’s direct turn toward God; the Mishnah says prayer should begin in solemn focus, with the pious waiting before they pray to direct their hearts.

The commentary says the prayer’s first direct word places God before the speaker’s own action; Augustine opens by addressing God in praise and describes the human heart as restless until it rests in God.
The commentary develops the owner, leading animal, pasture, and vulnerable wanderer within its herd imagery; the psalm names YHWH as shepherd and the speaker as a sheep who lacks nothing.
The commentary joins the service-path image to a later request for guidance; the shepherd psalm leads the sheep on right paths for his name’s sake.
The commentary pictures a worn traveler needing support and asks God for help; the psalmist walks through a deadly valley with the shepherd’s rod and staff as comfort.
The commentary contrasts a community that knows its owner with strays who lose the way; Ezekiel pictures YHWH searching for scattered sheep and rescuing them from where they have wandered.
The commentary’s root imagery includes the lost traveler and the herd animal gone astray; YHWH promises to seek the lost, bring back the strayed, bind the injured, and strengthen the weak.
The commentary’s augment links direct address to God’s answer to those who call; the psalm says YHWH hears those who call on him and saves them.

row.basis: our eyes on you for help
row.note: The commentary makes the aid request a separate act addressed to God; Jehoshaphat prays for the whole people, “we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.”
The commentary leaves the need for help open while making God its sole source; after the communal plea, Judah is told to stand and see the salvation YHWH will give.
The commentary describes the human speaker as belonging to the Lord of all creation; the psalm says the earth and all who dwell in it belong to YHWH.
The commentary says worship is addressed to God alone; Isaiah’s oracle has every knee bow to YHWH and every tongue swear allegiance to him.
The commentary recalls Moses asking God for Aaron’s help in the mission to Pharaoh; in Exodus God appoints Aaron to meet Moses and assist him as spokesman.

row.basis: God helps through a human agent
row.note: The commentary distinguishes asking God for help from receiving human assistance; God tells Moses to speak with Aaron and promises to help both of them speak.

row.basis: life and death belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary says a person belongs to God beyond scheduled acts of worship; Paul says that whether believers live or die, they belong to the Lord.
The commentary puts worship and asking aid side by side; Paul tells the community to bring every request to God with thanksgiving, joining petition to praise.
The commentary says worship is a continuing state and can be spoken in prayer; Hebrews calls believers to offer a continual sacrifice of praise through their lips.
The commentary moves from “we ask you for aid” to the next verse’s request for guidance; James tells anyone lacking wisdom to ask God, who gives generously.
The commentary leaves the aid requested open to every need; Peter tells believers to cast their anxieties on God because he cares for them.
The commentary reads “we” as a community that reaches beyond a solitary worshipper; Revelation gathers a multitude from every nation before the throne and the Lamb.
The commentary notes that the soul is first welcomed among God’s servants before entering the garden; Revelation depicts the gathered multitude serving God before his throne day and night.
The commentary develops the lost traveler, the herd, and the need for guidance and help; Revelation depicts the Lamb as shepherd leading the people to springs of living water.
The commentary places the community among God’s servants before naming the garden; Revelation’s final city is where God’s servants worship him and see his face.
The commentary says people or other means may assist while God remains the one ultimately asked for help; Hebrews describes angels as spirits sent to serve those who inherit salvation.
The commentary joins aid to worship and prayer; Paul says the Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes when they do not know how to pray.
The commentary evokes the strayed herd animal and the traveler who cannot find the way; Jesus’ parable has a shepherd leave the ninety-nine to search for one lost sheep.
The commentary’s image of a vulnerable traveler needing support is made concrete when the shepherd finds the lost sheep, puts it on his shoulders, and carries it home.
The commentary describes asking God for aid across all needs; Revelation says the gathered servants will hunger and thirst no more under the Lamb’s care.
The commentary distinguishes God as the one asked for help from those who can serve as instruments; Hebrews presents angels as agents sent to aid the heirs of salvation.
